frontmatter_description: Diagnose when a disagreement is resolved by BOTH sides adjusting their terms to build a jointly acceptable plan, versus one side influencing the other.
title: Negotiation, Concession, and Joint Plan
use_when: Use when two parties each hold a real stake in the outcome and the answer is the shape of the compromise both can accept.
Use when the best move requires giving up or trading something on BOTH sides, not just convincing one side.
Use when the scene asks for a split, swap, or middle plan that leaves each party with part of what they wanted.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when only one side wants something and the other is merely a target to be moved or convinced; that is persuasion, even if the speaker offers a sweetener.
Do not use when the task is to judge whether a split or exchange is fair rather than to reach a deal; that is fairness evaluation.
Do not use when one person is choosing among their own competing goals with no second party adjusting; that is goal-conflict arbitration.

Do not use when the central problem is a power gap and the move is command, permission, or deference; that is choosing a communication move across a power gap (the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability).
decision_variable: whether BOTH parties adjust their terms (bilateral concession) to form a joint plan, or only one side is moved
trigger_checklist: There are two parties whose wants conflict.
Each party holds a stake the other must accommodate, so neither can simply be talked out of it.
There is a tradeable or divisible dimension (time, money, tasks, turns, scope) to swap or split.
The accepted outcome leaves BOTH sides changed: each gives something and gets something.
workflow: State each party's interest and identify what each one will NOT give up versus what is flexible.
Test directionality: does only one party want a change (the other is a target)? If yes, route to persuasion and stop.
Find the tradeable or divisible dimension where the two interests can be swapped or split.
Construct a concession from EACH side that meets enough of both interests (I give X, you give Y).
Confirm the plan is jointly acceptable: each party is left better than no deal, and neither has simply submitted. Pick that option over any 'I win' or 'just convince them' option.

special_case.title: A sweetener is not a concession
special_case.rule: An offer of payment, a favor, or a reward to get one's own way is still one-way persuasion, because the other party's underlying want is bought off, not accommodated. It becomes negotiation only when BOTH parties hold a stake in the outcome and BOTH change their terms to reach it.

worked_example.scene: Xiao Ming needs Xiao Qiang's computer tonight, but Xiao Qiang has plans to game with friends. Option: 'You game elsewhere tonight, and you get my computer all day tomorrow.'
worked_example.question: Is this negotiation or persuasion?
worked_example.answer_logic: Only Xiao Ming wants a change; the original frame is one-sided ('how does Xiao Ming get the computer'). Offering milk tea or a reward is a sweetener that buys Xiao Qiang off, so it stays persuasion. It would be negotiation only if both held a genuine stake and both shifted terms to land a shared plan.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to persuasion if only one side wants the change and the other is being moved, paid, or convinced; offering a reward does not make it bilateral.
Exit to fairness/reciprocity if the task is to judge whether a distribution or exchange is fair, not to design a deal.
Exit to goal-conflict arbitration if a single person is weighing their own competing goals with no second party adjusting.

Exit to choosing a communication move across a power gap (the power-navigation / hierarchical-communication capability) if the live issue is a status gap and the move is command, permission, escalation, or deference.

references.route_signal: Route here when a scene asks how two parties, each with a real stake, swap or split a tradeable dimension so both end up with part of what they wanted.
hard_boundary: Bilateral adjustment is mandatory: both parties must change terms. One-way influence (even with a reward attached) is persuasion, not negotiation.
The target is the structure of the deal (who gives and gets what), not a verdict on whether an existing split is fair (that is fairness and reciprocity).
Two distinct parties are required; a single agent balancing their own goals is goal-conflict arbitration, not negotiation.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not treat every disagreement as negotiation; most persuasion stories have only one party who wants the change.
Do not count an offer of payment, milk tea, or a favor as a concession; a sweetener buys the other off and stays one-way.
Do not pick the option that fully wins for one side; negotiation needs a mutually acceptable middle.
Do not answer from a fairness verdict; the diagnostic is whether both sides change terms, not whether a split looks fair.
common_failure_modes: Labeling a one-way persuasion scene as negotiation because the speaker offers a reward or alternative.
Choosing the 'I get exactly what I want' option instead of the mutually acceptable plan.
Missing the tradeable dimension (time, turns, scope) that lets both sides give and get.
Confusing a fairness judgment about a split with the act of negotiating that split.

minimal_pair.case: Xiao Hong wants the amusement park; Dad objects to the noise; she suggests going to a park or zoo instead so everyone is happy.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: NOT negotiation -> persuasion. The frame is one-way ('how does Xiao Hong persuade her dad'); offering an alternative is a concession-flavored persuasion move, not two parties each shifting terms over a shared stake.

minimal_pair.case: Two teammates both want the single conference slot; one agrees to present later if the other prepares the slides and handles setup.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: IS negotiation. Both hold a real stake in the slot, and both change terms over a tradeable dimension (timing for labor), leaving each with part of what they wanted.

boundary_stress_test: If one side gives in and the other does not move at all, it is persuasion or compliance, not negotiation.
If a reward or favor is offered to get one's own way, the frame is still one-sided -> persuasion.
If the question is 'was this split fair?' rather than 'what deal do they strike?', route to fairness.
If a lone person is weighing their own competing goals, route to goal-conflict arbitration.
references.generalization_note: Generalizes to any two-party exchange where the diagnostic is reciprocal concession toward a shared plan, across friendships, work, family, and resource conflicts. The decisive test is always directionality: two genuine stakes plus mutual adjustment, versus one party being moved.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: Two parties each hold a real stake, a tradeable dimension exists, and the best answer is a plan where each gives something and gets something.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: Only one party wants the change and offers an alternative or reward; the other is a target to be persuaded, with no reciprocal stake or adjustment.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The task is to judge whether a split or exchange is fair, not to reach a deal, so route to fairness evaluation rather than negotiation.

notes: Keep the unit narrow: diagnose bilateral concession between two parties, not general agreement, persuasion, or fairness.
The primary confusion is persuasion; the decisive test is directionality (two stakes + mutual adjustment vs one party moved).
core_question: Find compromise, trades, and mutually acceptable plans under disagreement
